4.s: He sold the Record, Times, Herald and Express starting at Fifth and Central, explaining the prices and his two cents profit.
4.ch: Second session: boyhood, brothers and early road years
4.q: The Record, Times, and The Herald and The Express. And I first started out selling papers at the old Pacific Railroad 'cause it was right at Fifth and Central there, and we lived at Fourth Street, and I sold it at catching people coming off the train and going to the train, you see. Which I sold,…

4.t: Working for tailors as a delivery boy
4.s: Spikes describes cutting accessories and delivering bundles between pantsmakers, vestmakers and coatmakers for several tailors at a dollar and a half to three dollars a week.
4.ch: Second session: boyhood, brothers and early road years
4.q: After I stopped selling newspapers, I commenced to work in...uh, you know...messenger boy. I had a bicycle, and I get jobs for...in a tailor shop for delivering packages, and when it wasn't delivering packages, they'd give me a job where I'd cut all the linings, you know, for the coats...and…

4.t: Water boy on the Pacific Electric line
4.s: He carried water to track-laying crews building the red car line to Long Beach for a dollar a day.
4.ch: Second session: boyhood, brothers and early road years
4.q: Well, after that, I don't know. I went in the post office, but before I went in the post office, I worked on the railroad. When they built the big old red cars--you don't remember them--when they had the big old red cars that'd run to the beaches and all.

4.t: Special delivery messenger for the Los Angeles post office
4.s: On his bicycle he earned eight cents a letter and as much as sixty dollars a month at the main post office at Eighth and Spring.
4.ch: Second session: boyhood, brothers and early road years
4.q: Oh, I think it must have been about 1900 or 1901 or '2. I don't know. I know that after that I went in the post office as a messenger and that special delivery on my bicycle, and that was about 1902 or '3 or something like that. The old post office then was at Eighth and Spring Street, and...

232.t: Working as a section-gang water boy to save for Tuskegee
232.s: He badgers the railroad foreman Roy Martin into a water-boy job and saves money, planning to go to Tuskegee.
232.q: Anyway, I started school in Tuskegee, but before that, I was trying to figure out how was I going to go to school. There was a fellow with the railroad that had a section

232.t: Shining shoes in Muskogee and befriending Walter Thomas
232.s: In a Muskogee shine parlor he learns the trade's ways with help from Walter Thomas, who is saving for the Kansas Vocational School.
232.q: So I went to Muskogee and got a job in a shining parlor, and of course, I never will forget, my mother saying, son, whatever you do, do it good. But as a country boy, I

232.t: Dishwashing at Bishop's Cafe in Tulsa
232.s: Summer job washing dishes in a big Tulsa cafe while his mother stays with his brother in Sand Springs.
232.q: So we were just good buddies along and everything. When that was over, I went on then to finish school, a junior, and so that summer, before going to school, I came to Tulsa, my brother was teaching in Sand Springs, and I decided then that I was going to come up there and my mother said yes, she'll…

232.t: Wiring a duplex and working for Spot and Tate Electric
232.s: He wires a duplex without a license, a Black electrical contractor firm inspects it and hires him; the tape side ends.
232.ch: Tulsa bands, Trent, Holder and Kirk
232.q: Anyway, I was with this marching band, but I came on over to Tulsa and met some Tuskegee (inaudible), and one of them--two carpenters, they were a lot older than me, they were about my brother's age, and they were doing quite a bit of work, and when I told them I was a Tuskegee grad, they said…

427.t: Hustling junk, bottles and rags as a boy
427.s: The boys collected bottles, bones and rags for the junkyard, once seeing a dead horse there, and padded rag bags with rocks.
427.q: Yeah, you buy bones, bottles, rags and iron, copper ...stuff like that. One time I saw a whole dead horse in the junkyard. I couldn't figure that out. 'Course, was a law that wasn't too strict then so the fellow in the junkyard got by with it.

427.t: Taking the horse and wagon, and leading horses at the auction
427.s: He hitched a neighbor's horses and ran off with the wagon, and earned quarters leading horses at the Saturday auction.
427.q: back of the place that we lived at, where he kept his horses at, so I used to go down there and when he hitch 'em up, get a wagon. I would help him. So I learned how to hitch up the horses and the wagon by myself, so one day I decided that I was gonna take the wagon out myself. So I hitched up the…

427.t: The horse-and-wagon junk and ice business
427.s: With a sickly friend whose mother bought the horse and wagon, he hustled junk and sold ice they didn't know how to cut.
427.q: house all the time and listen to his Friday and Saturday night fish fries and listen to the piano and sing but I... But his mother would buy him anything 'cause he was real sickly, and I pumped it into his head...I said, "Get your mother to buy us a horse and wagon so we can go out and hustle. Get…

427.t: Junking with the wagon, a traffic cop's help, and the death of his friend
427.s: The boys hauled boxes past a friendly traffic cop; then the sick friend died and Turner became a pallbearer.
427.q: And then I go back to my friend's house that had the wagon and the horse. I say, "Well, let's go and hustle some more stuff...some more junk and stuff, and we gonna make us some money so we can buy us some ice cream cones!"

121.t: Shining shoes for Miss Josie at the riding academy
121.s: He started shining shoes at eight or nine; the story ends with Miss Josie's boots at Carrier's Riding Academy after a reel change.
121.q: I guess when I started shining shoes, I had to be around eight, nine years old. And... Where would you go? We would go up Jefferson Highway. We would go down to... First, we would stop in High Mills Bakery right there on... Right where the bank is, right near...

121.t: The black neighborhood in Shrewsbury and picking vegetables for pay
121.s: Which streets were black and white, and earning money picking okra and beans.
121.q: Yeah, well, right, right, right, on Causeway all the way back, it was all black. Now, on, on, on, on, on Claybone Drive was white. We used to call it subdivision, that was white over there. But Causeway, and, and, and, and the, and the, the side street, all that was, all that, you know, like…

876.s: He earned money lining barrels at a factory, with details of staves arriving by schooner.
876.q: Yeah. You see, the sugar barrels were made out of common staves. And they have a groove cut in for the head. Well, the sugar barrels, the staves were so thin that the groove was very shallow. So they had a lining. They put half way around on each side to reinforce the head, the grooves. And they…

876.t: Begging his stepfather to let him carry plaster
876.s: He asked to help his stepfather's plastering job, cried when refused, and was allowed to carry half a bucket.
876.q: Oh yes, I had to be an apprentice. I'll tell you what happened. My stepfather was contracting for himself. And we were living then on Telemachus between Borden and Henry Court. And that section wasn't well built up then. It just began to build that section up.

99.t: Hopping coal trains and driving mules in 1917-18
99.s: As the family gets poorer he hauls coal in the cold winter of 1917 and drives a mule team for $3.50 a day in the summer of 1918.
99.q: As I grew a little older, things got a little rougher for the family and I would go out and seek jobs. And I can remember back in 1918 -- back in 1917 rather -- was a real cold winter. And most kids would -- young boy -- young kids would hop freight trains, jump up on the coal cars and throw off…

99.t: Odd jobs to pay school tuition, fired for playing a piano
99.s: He makes school fires to avoid tuition, shines shoes, is fired from a piano company for playing the player piano, and gets a Missouri Pacific shop job in 1922.
99.q: A boy named Walter Baker and myself applied for the job of making fires in the stoves in the school in order to keep from paying the tuition. This was the only way I could go to school, because my father wasn't able to support me.

241.t: Rural boyhood: fieldwork and the sugar refinery
241.s: Thomas describes a rough country childhood working in the fields and the sugar refinery.
241.q: Well, I had to work. I had to work. Work in the field, you know what I mean? Work in the sugar refinery, you know what I mean? I do a different kind of job, you know? I do a different thing. I did a different thing. I did a different thing. I did everything, you know?

567.t: Odd jobs, selling papers and losing his legs on a streetcar
567.s: White says he never held regular work, farmed brick, sold newspapers and then jumped a car, which cost him his legs.
567.q: No, I never did work. I always did. I never did work because I had old people, or used to have, they had their own, you understand, was, was well, well, uh, well-doers, you understand. All I used to do, when they used to, I used to get money from them if I wanted anything. But I used to work,…

150.s: At ten or eleven he sold the Item for a penny on Washington Avenue, later the Louisiana Weekly, earning pennies for rent of a dollar a month.
150.ch: Irish Channel youth, newspapers and McDonogh 35
150.q: I remember mostly the white bands. I didn't see a Zulu parade until I was in my teens. See, because my mother kept close watch on me most of the time. I was in my teens. By her and my father being separated because I can remember when I was about 10, 11 years of age, my mother took sick and I…

251.t: Homemade balls and boyhood odd jobs
251.s: Kids made balls from stockings and earned nickels shining faucets, shopping and shining shoes.
251.q: Oh, we had ours. We used to make our balls. We used to take a stocking and rip it and just wrap it up and make a ball. We probably, sometime we put a little, a little, uh, small ball, a wooden ball or something, and then we'd wrap this thread around this ball and then sew it to keep it from, from…

83.t: Work ethic: stocking shelves and growing up in the grocery
83.s: Everyone worked; he stacked shelves, earned candy by behaving, and was punished for throwing clay.
83.q: Oh, sure. That was another thing my father and mother taught me. Everybody works. So, as a, as a small child, when I came home in the evening from school, as a small child, I stacked soap on the lower shelf because I couldn't reach anything else. Right. I put soup up on the middle shelf and maybe,…

665.t: Mother and sister delivering market for a butcher
665.s: Her mother and sister delivered market orders paid in meat.
665.q: Because my sister, she was small too. And my mother had them working for a man to market. He used to have to carry the people's market and the great big best. He'd put the names on them, the address. And they didn't have all these delivery trucks like they got. Now that was magazine market. A big…

194.t: Picking berries on farms as a child
194.s: As a child of six to nine he went by truck to farms across Louisiana to pick berries, hired at the street corner.
194.ch: CCC camp, field work and gambling
194.q: Yeah, that's when I was about six or seven, eight, nine years old. Where would you pick berries? I went through Hammond, Independent, Impostor Tool, Hall Bennett, Emet, Serento, Velma, Shiloh, Spencefield, Independent, Mopo, No showing off.

343.t: Shoeshine rates and working for Jim Hill at the fruit stand
343.s: He earned tips and gave money to his mother, then culled tomatoes for Jim Hill until being thrown into a garbage barrel.
343.q: I wasn’t very good businessman at the time, you know, I would just, you know, expect something. And apparently I did a good job because I’d get 15 to 20 cents, sometimes a quarter. And quite frankly, if I made over a couple of hours, let’s say three or four hours of work, I would take that money…

347.t: Improvising jazz and the Charleston boy who sold watermelon
347.s: Asked what he thinks about when soloing, Morant says he wants young people to tell their own story, and recalls his menial childhood jobs in Charleston.
347.q: Jazz. Because I improvise R&B and gospel. When I improvise jazz I’m thinking how fortunate it would be if the young people, especially the minority — I want to underscore that because they came up from the bottom line — the blacks, the Hispanics, some Jews — if only it would reflect on their…

111.t: The paper route with Arthur Hoseppian
111.s: Elvin recalls taking over a friend's paper route in junior high, giving papers free to families on welfare, and how friends fared in the war.
111.q: When I was going to junior high school, a friend of mine who lived right across the street from us his name was Arthur Hoseppian, he was Armenian, his whole family were Armenians, and my uncle used to speak Armenian and Greek. And I was fascinated by the languages, and he (Arthur) had a paper route…

589.t: Strict parents, after-school jobs and friend Bob Holmes
589.s: His parents allowed no idling; between church, prep school, homework and three jobs there was little time for friends beyond Bob Holmes, met through Geraldine Taylor.
589.ch: Growing up on the Near North Side
589.q: buildings going up, and that block was the last block to go down, and that building was the last building to go down. I used to take my kids and drive by and said, “I used to live there.” When I was in school, there wasn’t a lot of time for hanging out. My parents didn’t believe in hanging out. My…

565.t: Junior high gangs and working in his father's candy store
565.s: School was dangerous so he arrived late and left early; he worked the soda fountain and jukebox in El Mambo.
565.q: The junior high was 52, called at that time Thomas Knowlton, the Friendly School. On my first day in there, they were beating a kid to death. It was all gangs-related. Where I lived were the Lightnings, and by Jackson Avenue was the Rockets, then you had the Italians—the Huns. They were all…

80.t: Working in the Evergreen basket factory at ten or twelve
80.s: As a boy he and his brother made strawberry crates for 75 cents a day, and he describes how the pine logs were boiled and shaved.
80.ch: Boyhood in Evergreen and Calhoun school
80.q: Yes. Yes. Factory -- in fact I worked in there, at this factory. It was a basket factory where they made strawberry crates and all kinds of boxes and crates for this and for that, and I worked in there, my brother too, 75 cents a day.

1.t: Boyhood jobs: shoe shines, papers, pounding red brick
1.s: Danny describes the hustles of a Black boy: shining shoes, selling papers, working with peddlers and pounding red brick for sidewalk decoration.
1.ch: Becoming a musician: ukulele, clarinet and the Boozaire Kings
1.q: Everybody was so nice to the musicians. You're something special. You see that. So what the hell you gonna do? Now, you're a youngster, a Black youngster in New Orleans, and you figure, well, what'cha gonna do? From a kid you start shining shoes. You never even think of stealin' or takin' nothin'…

614.t: Living above a music store and early odd jobs
614.s: The family sometimes lived above stores, including a music store where he tried reeds, a grocery, and he worked at a men's clothing store in high school.
614.q: Another time I was -- we lived above a grocery store, and I used to do a little part time gigging there, filling five-pound sacks of sugar and things of that nature.

17.t: After high school: working to support the family, odd jobs
17.s: Cole and his brothers worked to send their sister through school; he was a tinsmith apprentice, errand boy, porter, elevator man and farm hand.
17.q: Oh well all right, say when I came out of high school I was 17, so in 1909, twelve years, that would make me how old, that would make me 9, 10, 11. No, 1909, so my first grade is when I was -- no it was in 1914, is that correct, yeah.

67.t: Summers in Atlanta: the 91 Theater and Mr. Bailey
67.s: Working summers at his aunt's laundry, he played cornet at the rowdy, dusty 91 Theater owned by Mr. Bailey, who was strict but a fine man.
67.q: No, before that. I would go to Atlanta, during the school's -- summertime, I'd go to Atlanta because I had an aunt there that was married to a Chinaman, and he had a laundry there so I used to go down in the summer and work in the laundry. And I played cornet at the 91 Theater, with Eddie Heywood…

166.s: As a boy he fetched sandwiches and cigarettes for musicians.
166.ch: Family background and the Tulsa music scene
166.q: No, I'd go to get sandwiches and things, you know, and go ahead and get cigarettes for them. 'Course at that time there was no such thing you couldn't sell cigarettes to kids, you know, because they just knew that you were going to get them for your parents or a grownup, you know. And that's how I…

231.t: Teenage jobs: tobacco hogsheads, shoe shining, restaurant
231.s: He describes hauling tobacco and keeping busy at every job to make money.
231.ch: Louisville, Buck and the carnival years
231.q: : ... about the bicycle and it didn't cost him nothing' cause I didn't grab it, let it go against me and ever after we did all right.

382.t: High school and limited work around Homestead
382.s: She finished high school in the late 1920s with little to do afterward in town.
382.ch: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
382.q: I finished high school but there wasn't that much to do around Homestead. I waited tables -- one of my aunts had a restaurant, one of my great-aunts -- my grandmother on my father's side had two sisters and a brother and they all had some sort of little business -- a restaurant or a little, what…

452.t: The drugstore job and the bicycle he had to pay for
452.s: Cobb gets a bicycle for a $7-a-week drugstore job, eats free ice cream, and finds it deducted from his first pay.
452.ch: First bands, illness and Houston life
452.q: But I had buddies; I had 2 buddies that went to work in the evenings. It was my first project, and I said, "Gee willikers, I got to get me a job, too" -- so first thing I did, I asked my mother to get me a bicycle; I could get a job working at the drugstore working in the evenings. And she…

386.t: Ashford's record store and shoeshine parlor
386.s: He describes the Central Track store with the shoeshine parlor where he shined shoes as the Charleston King.
386.q: Yeah, it was on the Central Track. And it was...actually, I don't think he could make it just selling records, do you understand? So he had a shoeshine parlor-- sold shoelaces and things. And he had about seven guys that shined shoes. And I used to shine shoes there because the people wanted the…

30.t: Working as a cigar maker and photo engraver as a boy
30.s: Before music he worked at 11 or 12 for his uncle in cigars, disliked the conditions, then at 13 or 14 worked for the Russian photo engraver Romansky making prints for the Sunday paper.
30.q: Yeah. I was a cigar maker. See, I was starting used to work for my uncle first -- in the cigar business, and I started from the ground up. I started to strip tobacco, sift it, sweep the building, and I started to breaking bunches. Then I started to roll them. Then I started making them for myself.…

125.t: A failed job as a dishwasher and the idea of caddying
125.s: Wanting money at twelve, Thompson tried dishwashing, quit almost at once, and then heard of caddying.
125.q: It was during this time there was a combination of need to enhance the bankroll, you know, my father gave me things that I needed, nice clothes, and in return I had to be sure and take care of them. So I didn't have an abundance of clothes, but I had nice clothes for church and for outings and I…

79.t: Summer jobs and the trip to Lincoln
79.s: With a buddy he mowed lawns and dug ditches to ease the family burden. His mother packed a week of food for the four-hour, 125-mile trip.
79.ch: Boyhood in Webster Groves and early roadhouse work
79.q: We'd mow the lawns and that sort of thing and then we got game. We got real game and we went to dig some ditches because digging the ditches paid a whole lot of money, you know. And, at 12 o'clock ... through.
